lesson.title: The Number Nobody Reads Until Something Melts
lesson.summary: A component's power rating is the maximum heat it can safely dissipate before it is damaged, and exceeding it, even with an otherwise perfectly valid circuit, is a common cause of real world failures.
lesson.body:
Power was defined earlier through P = IV, and power dissipation described how a resistive element converts electrical energy into heat rather than useful work. Every real component built around that same physics, resistors, capacitors, transistors, has a limit on how much of that heat it can safely produce and shed before something inside it is damaged. That limit is the component's power rating, printed on the part or specified in its datasheet, almost always in watts.

The physical reason for the limit is straightforward: heat generated inside the component has to be conducted or radiated away fast enough to keep its internal temperature below a safe maximum. Run a part below its rating, and heat generated equals heat removed, temperature settles at a safe steady value. Run it above the rating, and heat builds up faster than it can escape, internal temperature climbs until something fails: solder joints crack, plastic packaging deforms, resistive material drifts out of tolerance, or in the worst case the part burns out entirely.

Worked example: a standard 220 ohm resistor is commonly rated for 0.25 watts, a quarter watt part. Using P = I squared R and P = V squared over R, the maximum current it can handle on its own is I = square root of P over R = square root of 0.25 divided by 220 = square root of 0.0011364, about 0.0337 amps, or 33.7 milliamps, and the maximum voltage across it alone is V = square root of P times R = square root of 0.25 times 220 = square root of 55, about 7.42 volts. Now suppose a careless design connects this same 220 ohm resistor directly across a 9 volt battery with nothing else in the circuit. The actual power dissipated is P = V squared over R = 81 divided by 220, about 0.368 watts, roughly 47 percent above the 0.25 watt rating. That resistor will run hot, its value may drift, and with sustained use it risks outright failure, even though nothing about Ohm's law was violated, the circuit is simply asking more of the part than it was built to give.

Different components get rated differently. Resistors are rated in straightforward watts, since dissipating heat is their entire job. Capacitors, by contrast, are primarily rated by working voltage rather than power, since an ideal capacitor draws no steady current, but real capacitors carrying ripple current do generate heat through internal losses, which shows up as a separate ripple current rating rather than a simple wattage, a detail the real versus ideal components chapter explains in more depth.

The rating on a datasheet is not a target to design toward, it marks the edge past which damage begins. Treating it as a hard ceiling with no room to spare is risky in practice, since temperature, tolerance, and aging all push a real design around that edge. Building in a deliberate safety margin below the rated limit is exactly the practice the next chapter, component derating, formalizes.
